talks.title: IoT Hacking Stories in Real Life
talks.teaser: Shares real-world case studies and practical lessons learned from testing and hacking consumer IoT devices.
talks.summary:
In this practical briefing from the DEF CON Safe Mode IoT Village, an embedded security penetration tester shares real-world case studies assessing consumer and enterprise smart devices. Opening at 00:00, the presenter explores the pervasive design shortcuts and security anti-patterns that plague modern IoT products.

At 06:00, the speaker details physical attack surfaces, illustrating how unencrypted UART and JTAG interfaces left enabled on production hardware allow attackers to obtain root interactive shells.

At 12:02 and 16:04, the presentation exposes severe cloud backend vulnerabilities, demonstrating how hardcoded API keys, insecure device pairing routines, and broken object level authorization (BOLA) in cloud management APIs permit unauthorized attackers to remotely hijack smart home devices and access sensitive user profile data. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Hacking Smart Devices for Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Explores vulnerability discovery techniques and exploitation workflows targeting connected smart devices.
talks.summary:
Barak Sternberg presents research into smart building automation ecosystems, focusing on devices manufactured by HDL Automation and their cloud control platform, HDL On Pro [08:52]. While smart buildings often isolate physical controller hardware on local serial buses like RS-485 and Dynet [04:20], modern deployments increasingly rely on cloud-connected bridge controllers to allow remote management via mobile applications [12:57]. Sternberg demonstrates that rather than spending weeks reverse engineering local hardware, auditing cloud APIs and web services often reveals severe vulnerabilities that expose thousands of physical buildings globally [17:12].

The talk details multiple critical vulnerabilities uncovered across the HDL cloud infrastructure. Sternberg explains a broken authentication flaw in the password reset endpoint where tampering with the email parameter allowed an attacker to reset any registered user's credentials and take over their account [21:26]. Additionally, he highlights SQL injection vulnerabilities within public API endpoints—specifically the `device by region list` endpoint—that allowed exfiltration of sensitive database records, user profiles, and device registration tokens [25:44]. Insecure direct object references (IDOR) further permitted attackers to scrape customer records and link users directly to their physical devices [34:32].

Sternberg shows how these vulnerabilities can be weaponized into physical attacks against smart facilities, demonstrating how an attacker can hijack smart home configurations, link lighting switches to blast HVAC heating up to 45°C, and disable intrusion sensors [38:44]. The presentation concludes with a review of the responsible disclosure process conducted with HDL Automation, outlining the remediation steps implemented to secure the cloud platform and offering defense strategies for IoT cloud architectures.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: NAND Flash Recovering File Systems
talks.teaser: Details techniques for dumping raw NAND flash chips, reconstructing wear-leveled blocks, and recovering embedded filesystems.
talks.summary:
In this advanced hardware hacking tutorial from the DEF CON Safe Mode IoT Village, an embedded researcher demonstrates a complete methodology for extracting and reconstructing file systems from raw NAND flash memory. Opening at 00:00, the presenter explains how NAND flash architecture differs fundamentally from SPI NOR flash due to out-of-band data areas, wear leveling, and bad block tables.

At 16:01 and 32:02, the speaker demonstrates chip-off hardware techniques, desoldering TSOP and BGA surface-mount packages using hot air stations, cleaning solder pads, and reading raw bitstreams with dedicated chip programmers.

At 48:00, the walkthrough demonstrates software reconstruction, showing how to strip error-correcting code (ECC) parity blocks, handle data scrambling, and assemble raw dumps into mountable SquashFS and UBIFS partition images to extract proprietary firmware binaries and configuration secrets. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Getting Started Building an IoT Hardware Hacking Lab
talks.teaser: Guides defenders and researchers through assembling an affordable hardware hacking workbench with essential tools and equipment.
talks.summary:
Deral Heiland, IoT Research Lead at Rapid7, delivers a comprehensive, practical walkthrough on building an IoT hardware hacking and firmware analysis lab suitable for beginners through advanced practitioners [00:00]. He begins by addressing workspace ergonomics and physical disassembly essentials, covering screwdrivers (security bits, spudgers), precision tweezers, digital microscopes, and borescopes or USB pen cameras used to inspect confined interior spaces without destroying device enclosures [14:20].

Heiland dives into soldering and desoldering tools, discussing temperature-controlled irons (Weller stations, TS100 portable irons), hot air rework stations, solder flux, desoldering braid, and low-melt bismuth alloys like Chip Quik for removing delicate surface-mount components [07:03]. Moving to hardware interfaces, he explains how to extract firmware from flash memory chips using programmers like the TL866II Plus, SOIC test clips, and low-cost CH341A adapters [36:28]. For communications analysis and protocol reverse engineering, he evaluates budget-friendly USB-to-UART serial adapters, logic analyzers (comparing 8-channel $12 clones running Sigrok/PulseView against high-end Saleae units) [44:22], and hardware debuggers like the SEGGER J-Link and ST-Link for ARM JTAG/SWD interfaces [51:21].

The session includes practical lab techniques, such as using 30 AWG wire-wrapping wire and UV-cure solder mask or hot glue to reinforce micro-soldered tap wires against accidental tearing [01:06:02]. Heiland concludes by advising researchers on how to source cheap consumer targets from thrift stores and online marketplaces to practice board identification, pinout tracing, and firmware dumping.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Stepped on a Nail
talks.teaser: Presents an embedded hardware research case study dissecting device security architecture and unexpected failure modes.
talks.summary:
In this consumer device security presentation from the DEF CON Safe Mode IoT Village, researcher Matt presents "Stepped on a Nail," an investigative case study uncovering systemic vulnerabilities in consumer smart products and mobile companion apps. Opening at 00:00, Matt discusses the widespread adoption of inexpensive internet-connected hardware in consumer households.

At 15:00, the talk examines the acute lack of consumer security awareness and the absence of vendor accountability for ongoing firmware maintenance. At 30:03 and 45:01, Matt demonstrates reverse engineering companion mobile applications and network communication protocols, uncovering exposed cloud endpoints, unencrypted diagnostic telemetry, and hardcoded authentication tokens.

Concluding at 01:00:00, the presenter examines the broader privacy implications of consumer IoT proliferation, warning that unvetted smart devices facilitate mass data collection and erode digital civil liberties. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: VULNtron: 4 CVEs Turn a Teleconference Bot into a Spy
talks.teaser: Chains four CVEs in a commercial telepresence robot to achieve remote code execution and covert surveillance.
talks.summary:
Mark Bereza presents an in-depth vulnerability assessment of the Temi telepresence robot—an autonomous mobile video conferencing robot widely adopted in hospitals, corporate offices, and Southeast Asian enterprise environments [03:53]. Bereza demonstrates how chaining four distinct vulnerabilities across the Temi Android companion application, cloud messaging brokers, and backend REST APIs allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to completely hijack the robot, secretly control its motors, and stream video and audio without alerting occupants [00:17].

The vulnerabilities form an exploit chain that dismantles each security barrier in sequence. First, Bereza analyzes the integrated Agora Video SDK and discovers hardcoded credentials (CVE-2020-14470), specifically an Agora App ID deployed without token authentication [14:06]. Second, he exploits an origin validation weakness in the Temi Android APK, enabling arbitrary modification and repackaging of the application without client integrity checks [18:33]. Third, he identifies missing access controls on the Temi MQTT broker, where user topic identifiers were derived from simple MD5 hashes of user phone numbers, allowing attackers to subscribe to other users' call notification channels [21:39]. Fourth, he uncovers an authentication bypass in the Temi REST API (`syncContacts`), where manipulating owner IDs allowed an attacker to self-authorize as an administrator [26:01].

Bereza concludes with an end-to-end demonstration where a modified client connects to a victim robot, mutes the attacker's own microphone and camera feed, and silently navigates the environment while eavesdropping on confidential meetings [37:08]. The talk highlights the necessity of server-side authorization enforcement, dynamic token validation, and defense-in-depth in enterprise IoT robotics.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Introduction to U-Boot Interaction and Hacking
talks.teaser: Walks through interacting with the U-Boot bootloader via serial console to extract firmware and alter boot parameters.
talks.summary:
In this comprehensive hardware hacking workshop from the DEF CON Safe Mode IoT Village, an embedded systems researcher delivers an in-depth guide to interacting with and compromising the Universal Boot Loader (U-Boot) on embedded Linux hardware. Opening at 00:00, the presenter outlines the boot sequence of typical embedded systems.

At 19:00 and 38:00, the speaker demonstrates hardware interception techniques, showing how monitoring serial UART consoles and applying targeted pin glitches on flash memory data lines during startup disrupts the boot counter, dropping the terminal into an interactive U-Boot prompt.

At 57:01, the presenter illustrates manipulating bootloader environment variables, demonstrating how to modify the bootargs string to inject init=/bin/sh and boot modified kernel images from RAM or network TFTP servers. Concluding at 01:16:01 with a travel router case study, the session provides a dependable playbook for gaining unauthenticated root access to embedded Linux appliances. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Vulnerability Trends in the Supply Chain
talks.teaser: Examines recurring vulnerability patterns, outdated third-party SDKs, and component reuse across IoT supply chains.
talks.summary:
Parker Wiksell explores the complex landscape of IoT firmware supply chain security, analyzing why hardware manufacturers frequently deploy firmware containing critical vulnerabilities they are entirely unaware of [00:00]. Wiksell explains that device firmware is rarely written from scratch; instead, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) rely on third-party system-on-chip (SoC) vendor software developer kits (SDKs), board support packages, and open-source software (OSS) libraries [05:22]. This cascading multi-tier dependency chain creates significant blind spots where vulnerabilities in foundational components propagate undetected across hundreds of consumer and enterprise products.

The presentation illustrates the breakdown of traditional vulnerability tracking systems, emphasizing that the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) matching fail to accurately reflect embedded software components [15:54]. Using examples such as the Treck TCP/IP stack (Ripple20) and legacy forks of OpenWrt, Wiksell shows how vulnerable networking stacks and hardcoded backdoors persist in shipping hardware for decades [21:34]. He presents empirical findings from automated firmware analysis across thousands of production images, revealing widespread anti-patterns including copy-pasted configuration files with private test DNS servers (`192.168.0.7`, `someone.com`) [32:34], enabled web server directory auto-indexing [38:03], and root debug consoles left active in `inittab`.

Wiksell emphasizes that securing the IoT ecosystem requires comprehensive Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs), binary software composition analysis (SCA), and vendor accountability throughout the supply chain [41:28]. He urges organizations to actively inspect binary firmware rather than relying on vendor security claims.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Hella Booters, Why IoT Botnets Aren't Going Anywhere
talks.teaser: Analyzes the persistent economics, attack vectors, and lifecycle of IoT botnets driving modern DDoS-for-hire services.
talks.summary:
In this unfiltered presentation from the DEF CON Safe Mode IoT Village, the speaker analyzes the illicit underground ecosystem powering IoT botnets and commercial DDoS-for-hire platforms ("booters"). Opening at 00:00, the presenter explores the criminal economy surrounding large-scale distributed denial-of-service operations.

At 11:01 and 22:00, the talk examines threat actor communities operating across Discord and Telegram, tracing how amateur operators fork and customize Mirai source variants to recruit thousands of compromised IoT nodes into persistent bot networks.

At 33:01, the speaker investigates the technical root causes of widespread device exploitation, spotlighting outdated vendor toolchains, unauthenticated remote services, and hardcoded administrative credentials. Concluding at 44:00, the presenter emphasizes that until manufacturers face economic accountability for vulnerable hardware, IoT botnets will remain an enduring threat to internet infrastructure. talks.title: Pandemic in Plaintext
talks.teaser: Reveals how medical and consumer IoT devices deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic transmitted sensitive data in plaintext.
talks.summary:
RF engineer Troy Brown (wave_guide) shares findings from an investigation into hospital wireless communications during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic [00:01]. Seeking independent ground-truth data on ICU bed shortages and patient hospitalization rates, Brown turned to unencrypted radio paging protocols (POCSAG and FLEX) operating in the 929–931 MHz frequency band, which are ubiquitous across North American healthcare networks [02:24].

Brown challenges the common institutional claim that intercepting and decoding hospital pager transmissions constitutes a "sophisticated cyberattack" [04:50]. Using an inexpensive RTL-SDR dongle and open-source decoding tools like multimon-ng, he intercepted over 52 days of radio traffic, recording 17,286 decoded messages [15:35]. The captured transmissions contained egregious HIPAA violations broadcast in clear plaintext over the airwaves: 1,852 bed coordination requests containing patient full names, ages, room assignments, and physician details, along with 2,077 diagnostic messages including 1,219 explicit COVID-19 diagnoses, mechanical ventilation orders, and mortality notifications [15:41].

The talk contrasts hospital investments in internal network firewalls and enterprise HIPAA compliance software with the total absence of encryption on RF paging systems [10:11]. Brown demonstrates that commercial paging telemetry systems aggregate this unencrypted RF data into real-time hospital administrative dashboards [18:16]. He concludes with an urgent call for healthcare administrators, privacy regulators, and legal authorities to decommission unencrypted pagers in favor of secure, end-to-end encrypted mobile messaging solutions [19:45].

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)
